intro.html: Fear comes in sizes. A qualm is a small twinge of doubt; dread is a heavy fear of something on its way; a phobia is a strong, lasting fear of one thing. This topic also gives you verbs for what frightening things do to us: they unnerve, daunt, intimidate and perturb.

Feelings (nouns): dread, qualm, misgiving, foreboding, phobia, consternation. What scares or worries us (verbs): unnerve, daunt, intimidate, perturb. Ask two questions: how strong is the fear, and is it about now or about what is coming?

words.def: great fear of something that is coming
words.ex: Kai felt a growing {dread} as the dentist’s door creaked open.
words.ctx: The class had looked forward to the field trip for weeks, but as the bus crawled up the narrow cliff road, their excitement turned to {dread}.
words.etym: From an Old English verb meaning “to fear.”

mn.cue: DREAD: the thing under the BED
mn.text: As bedtime nears, Pip is full of {dread}: he is sure something is hiding under his bed. (It is only the cat.)

labels.text: DREAD of what’s under the BED

scene.alt: A frightened boy stares at his bed, sure something is hiding under it; it is only a cat.

words.def: a sudden uneasy feeling, especially a doubt about whether something is right
words.ex: Rosa had no {qualms} about eating the last cookie; she had baked them all herself.
words.ctx: Lila agreed to keep her friend’s secret, but later she felt a {qualm}: what if staying quiet meant that someone got hurt?
words.note: A qualm is a twinge of doubt or conscience, not a full fear. People often say they have no qualms about doing something.

mn.cue: QU + CALM: calm, with a QUestion
mn.text: Zoe reaches calmly for the cookie jar before dinner, then pauses: “Should I?” That little twinge of doubt is a {qualm}.

scene.alt: A girl reaches for the cookie jar before dinner and stops, unsure whether she should.

words.def: a feeling of doubt or worry about whether something will turn out well
words.ex: Despite her {misgivings}, Ada let her son ride the giant roller coaster.
words.ctx: The plan looked fine on paper, yet Omar had {misgivings}: the bridge was old, the river was high and the map was twenty years out of date.
words.etym: From the old verb misgive, as in “my heart misgives me”: to fill with doubt.

mn.text: Marcus holds out the car keys to Jonah for his first drive alone, but his hand hesitates: he has a {misgiving} about giving them.

scene.alt: A worried father hesitates as he hands the car keys to his eager teenage son.

words.def: to make someone lose courage or calm
words.ex: The creaking floorboards {unnerved} the new babysitter.
words.ctx: The goalie was usually steady, but the roaring crowd {unnerved} him; his hands shook, and he let in two easy goals.
words.etym: From un- (taking away) + nerve, in its old sense of strength and courage.

mn.text: Dev boasted he would jump from the high rock into the river, but standing at the edge, he loses his nerve. The height {unnerves} him.

scene.alt: A teen with shaking knees stands on a high rock above a river, too scared to jump.

words.def: to make someone feel discouraged or afraid to try
words.ex: The steep trail did not {daunt} Granny Mae; she reached the top before anyone else.
words.ctx: Most climbers would have turned back at the icy cliff, but the long drop did not {daunt} Tia, who checked her ropes and started up.
words.etym: From Old French danter, from Latin domitare, “to tame.”
words.note: Daunt (to discourage) is not taunt (to mock). Daunting is common as an adjective: a daunting task.

mn.cue: DAUNT = DON’T: the mountain says DON’T
mn.text: The giant mountain seems to say “Don’t!” to tiny Felix at its foot. Its size {daunts} him, and he almost turns back.

scene.alt: A small hiker with a backpack stares up at a huge mountain, discouraged.

words.def: to frighten someone, often to make them do what you want
words.ex: The big dog’s deep bark {intimidated} the mail carrier.
words.ctx: Rex tried to {intimidate} the younger players by glaring and stomping, but they simply ignored him and went on with their game.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin intimidare, “to make afraid”: in (into) + timidus (fearful).

mn.text: The barn cat puffs up and hisses, and the little mouse turns timid and backs away from the cheese. The cat {intimidates} the mouse.

scene.alt: A puffed-up cat hisses at a little mouse, which backs away from a piece of cheese.

words.def: a feeling that something bad is going to happen
words.ex: Watching the black clouds gather, Sven had a {foreboding} that the fishing trip would end early.
words.ctx: Nothing seemed wrong in the old house, yet Maya was filled with {foreboding}; the silence felt heavy, and she could not shake the sense that trouble was near.
words.etym: From fore (ahead) + bode, an old word meaning “to announce or foretell.”

mn.cue: FORE-BOAT-ing: a bad feeling before the BOAT trip
mn.text: Before the boat trip, Sven sees black clouds rolling in and feels sure that trouble is coming. That feeling is a {foreboding}.

scene.alt: A fisherman on the dock looks worriedly at dark storm clouds rolling in over the sea.

words.def: a strong, lasting fear of one thing, often far beyond any real danger
words.ex: Felix has a {phobia} of elevators, so he always takes the stairs.
words.ctx: Ivy’s {phobia} was out of all proportion to any real danger: even a photo of a tiny, harmless spider made her heart pound.
words.etym: From Greek phobos, “fear, panic.” The ending -phobia names many fears: acrophobia is a fear of heights.

mn.cue: FOE-BEE-a: every BEE is her FOE
mn.text: To Greta, every bee is a foe: she has a {phobia} of bees and runs from even the smallest one.

labels.text: FOE-BEE-a: the BEE is her FOE

scene.alt: A woman runs in terror from a small, smiling bee in the garden.

words.def: sudden alarm and confusion; shocked dismay
words.ex: To the baker’s {consternation}, the wedding cake slid right off the cart.
words.ctx: The lights went out just as the play reached its final scene, and {consternation} swept through the theater: people gasped, phones lit up and the actors froze.
words.etym: From Latin consternatio, “dismay, alarm,” from consternare, “to throw into confusion.”

mn.cue: the whole NATION STARES in alarm
mn.text: At the town fair, the giant cake begins to topple, and the whole crowd stares and gasps in alarm: {consternation}!

scene.alt: A crowd at a fair gasps in alarm as a giant cake starts to topple off its table.

words.def: to make someone worried or upset
words.ex: It {perturbed} Grandpa Gus that the newspaper had not come by eight.
words.ctx: The pilot’s calm voice usually soothed the passengers, so when he sounded rushed and tense, it {perturbed} them more than the bumpy air did.
words.etym: From Latin perturbare, “to throw into confusion”: per (thoroughly) + turbare (to disturb), the root of disturb and turbulent.

mn.text: Sami’s drumming next door keeps disturbing Grandpa’s crossword until he can’t think straight. The noise {perturbs} him.

scene.alt: A grumpy grandfather tries to read his newspaper while a boy bangs loudly on a drum.

how strong
about what
rows: whether a plan will turn out well
trouble that is on its way
something that has just gone wrong
after.cap: Six fears, from a twinge to a shock.

after.html: The four verbs differ, too. To unnerve is to take away someone’s courage or calm; to daunt is to discourage someone from trying; to intimidate is to frighten someone, often to push them around; to perturb is to worry or upset. Don’t mix up daunt and taunt: to taunt is to mock. And a qualm is only a twinge of doubt, usually about whether something is right.

opts.s: Tia felt a {qualm} about reading her sister’s diary, so she closed it and put it back on the shelf.
opts.why: A small twinge of doubt about whether something is right is a qualm.

items.q: The size of the cleanup did not ______ the volunteers; they started work at dawn. Which word fits?
items.why: To daunt is to discourage. To taunt is to mock, which does not fit; qualm and foreboding are nouns.

items.q: True or false: a qualm is a powerful, lasting terror.
items.why: False. A qualm is a sudden twinge of doubt or unease, often about whether something is right. A strong, lasting fear is a phobia.
Phobos is Greek for fear, so acrophobia is a fear of heights.

items.q: Which word names a feeling that trouble is on the way, before anything has gone wrong?
items.why: A foreboding comes before the trouble (fore- means before). Consternation is the shock after something goes wrong.

items.q: Type the word built from in- + timid that means to frighten someone, often to make them do what you want.
items.why: To intimidate is to make someone timid, often to push them around.
